'''Peter Anthony Koopman''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|FAA}} (born 3 December 1959) is an Australian biologist best known for his role in the discovery and study of the mammalian Y-chromosomal sex-determining gene, Sry.<ref name="Gubbay 1990">{{Cite journal|last1=Gubbay|first1=John|last2=Collignon|first2=Jérôme|last3=Koopman|first3=Peter|last4=Capel|first4=Blanche|last5=Economou|first5=Androulla|last6=Münsterberg|first6=Andrea|last7=Vivian|first7=Nigel|last8=Goodfellow|first8=Peter|last9=Lovell-Badge|first9=Robin|date=July 1990|title=A gene mapping to the sex-determining region of the mouse Y chromosome is a member of a novel family of embryonically expressed genes|journal=Nature|volume=346|issue=6281|pages=245–250|doi=10.1038/346245a0|pmid=2374589|bibcode=1990Natur.346..245G|s2cid=4270188|issn=0028-0836}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Koopman|first1=Peter|last2=Münsterberg|first2=Andrea|last3=Capel|first3=Blanche|last4=Vivian|first4=Nigel|last5=Lovell-Badge|first5=Robin|date=November 1990|title=Expression of a candidate sex-determining gene during mouse testis differentiation|journal=Nature|volume=348|issue=6300|pages=450–452|doi=10.1038/348450a0|pmid=2247150|bibcode=1990Natur.348..450K|s2cid=4322050|issn=0028-0836}}</ref><ref name="Koopman 1991">{{Cite journal|last1=Koopman|first1=Peter|last2=Gubbay|first2=John|last3=Vivian|first3=Nigel|last4=Goodfellow|first4=Peter|last5=Lovell-Badge|first5=Robin|date=May 1991|title=Male development of chromosomally female mice transgenic for Sry|journal=Nature|volume=351|issue=6322|pages=117–121|doi=10.1038/351117a0|pmid=2030730|bibcode=1991Natur.351..117K|s2cid=3331979|issn=0028-0836}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=The University of Queensland |title=UQ Researchers |url=http://researchers.uq.edu.au/researcher/255}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Peter Anthony Koopman was born on 3 December 1959 in [[Geelong, Victoria]], to Dutch immigrant parents, and raised in the coastal town of [[Torquay, Victoria]]. He attended Oberon High School in Geelong, where he was School Captain. He studied science at the [[University of Melbourne]] from 1977 to 1979, majoring in genetics, and was a resident of Janet Clarke Hall. He undertook BSc Honours research at the Birth Defects Research Institute (now the [[Murdoch Children's Research Institute]]) at the Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne, under the supervision of [[Richard Cotton (geneticist)|Richard (Dick) Cotton]], and graduated with First Class Honours.

Continuing to work with Cotton, his PhD focused on stem cell differentiation [[in vitro]]. During this time, he also studied Japanese, Fine Arts and Dutch language and literature, receiving a BA degree from the University of Melbourne in 1985.

He was awarded a [[Doctor of Science]] (DSc) from the [[University of Queensland]] in July 2018.

== Career and research ==
{{Scholia}}

=== Discovery of Sry and the genetics of sex determination ===

In 1988, Koopman was recruited to the Medical Research Council's [[National Institute for Medical Research]] at Mill Hill, London, working first with [[Anne McLaren]], then joining a team led by [[Robin Lovell-Badge]] to search for the Y chromosomal sex-determining gene. Koopman demonstrated that activity of mouse homologues of the existing candidate, ZFY, was not consistent with a role in [[Sexual differentiation in humans|sex determination]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Koopman|first1=Peter|last2=Gubbay|first2=John|last3=Collignon|first3=Jérôme|last4=Lovell-Badge|first4=Robin|date=December 1989|title=Zfy gene expression patterns are not compatible with a primary role in mouse sex determination|journal=Nature|volume=342|issue=6252|pages=940–942|doi=10.1038/342940a0|pmid=2480529|bibcode=1989Natur.342..940K|s2cid=4303582|issn=0028-0836}}</ref> Lovell-Badge's team, collaborating with Peter Goodfellow and colleagues at the Imperial Cancer Research Fund in London, discovered a new candidate gene, Sry.<ref name="Gubbay 1990" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sinclair|first1=Andrew H.|last2=Berta|first2=Philippe|last3=Palmer|first3=Mark S.|last4=Hawkins|first4=J. Ross|last5=Griffiths|first5=Beatrice L.|last6=Smith|first6=Matthijs J.|last7=Foster|first7=Jamie W.|last8=Frischauf|first8=Anna-Maria|last9=Lovell-Badge|first9=Robin|date=July 1990|title=A gene from the human sex-determining region encodes a protein with homology to a conserved DNA-binding motif|journal=Nature|volume=346|issue=6281|pages=240–244|doi=10.1038/346240a0|pmid=1695712|bibcode=1990Natur.346..240S|s2cid=4364032|issn=0028-0836|url=http://rcin.org.pl/Content/66315|archive-date=22 March 2021|access-date=11 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322201918/http://rcin.org.pl/Content/66315/WA248_85922_P-I-2524_derra-meandry_o.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Koopman and colleagues injected Sry into fertilized XX mouse eggs which as a result developed as males, thus proving the male sex-determining role of Sry.<ref name="Koopman 1991" /> The discovery is regarded as one of the major achievements in molecular genetics in the 20th century.

Much of Koopman's subsequent research has focused on understanding how Sry acts to direct the formation of testes in the embryo, triggering male development. This work has involved the identification and/or study of a large number of other genes involved in development of the testes or ovaries.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://espace.library.uq.edu.au/view/UQ:cb42c21|title=UQ eSpace|website=espace.library.uq.edu.au|access-date=2018-10-10}}</ref>

=== Sox genes ===
Establishing his own research group<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://imb.uq.edu.au/disorders-of-sex-development-infertility-and-testicular-cancer|title=Institute for Molecular Bioscience - University of Queensland|work=Institute for Molecular Bioscience|access-date=2018-10-10}}</ref> at the University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia in 1992, Koopman set out to discover new members of a growing family of genes related to Sry – "Sox" genes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wright|first1=Edwina M.|last2=Snopek|first2=Bernadette|last3=Koopman|first3=Peter|date=1993|title=Seven new members of theSoxgene family expressed during mouse development|journal=Nucleic Acids Research|volume=21|issue=3|pages=744|doi=10.1093/nar/21.3.744|pmid=8441686|pmc=309180|issn=0305-1048}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Koopman P, Bullejos M, Bowles J. |title=Regulation of male sexual development by Sry and Sox9. |journal=Journal of Experimental Zoology |date=2001 |volume=290 |issue=5 |pages=463–474 |pmid=11555853|doi=10.1002/jez.1089 |bibcode=2001JEZ...290..463K }}</ref> Among the first discoveries was Sox9,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wright|first1=Edwina|last2=Hargrave|first2=Murray R.|last3=Christiansen|first3=Jeffrey|last4=Cooper|first4=Leanne|last5=Kun|first5=Jutta|last6=Evans|first6=Timothy|last7=Gangadharan|first7=Uma|last8=Greenfield|first8=Andy|last9=Koopman|first9=Peter|date=January 1995|title=The Sry-related gene Sox9 is expressed during chondrogenesis in mouse embryos|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=9|issue=1|pages=15–20|doi=10.1038/ng0195-15|pmid=7704017|s2cid=22654180|issn=1061-4036}}</ref> a key regulator of skeletal and testis development, which carries mutations in humans with the skeletal disorder [[campomelic dysplasia]] and associated XY sex reversal.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Foster|first1=Jamie W.|last2=Dominguez-Steglich|first2=Marina A.|last3=Guioli|first3=Silvana|last4=Kwok|first4=Cheni|last5=Weller|first5=Polly A.|last6=Stevanović|first6=Milena|last7=Weissenbach|first7=Jean|last8=Mansour|first8=Sahar|last9=Young|first9=Ian D.|date=December 1994|title=Campomelic dysplasia and autosomal sex reversal caused by mutations in an SRY-related gene|journal=Nature|volume=372|issue=6506|pages=525–530|doi=10.1038/372525a0|pmid=7990924|bibcode=1994Natur.372..525F|s2cid=1472426|issn=0028-0836}}</ref>

Koopman's group also discovered Sox18,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hosking|first1=Brett M.|last2=Muscat|first2=George E.O.|last3=Koopman|first3=Peter A.|last4=Dowhan|first4=Dennis H.|last5=Dunn|first5=Timothy L.|date=1995|title=Trans-activation and DNA-binding properties of the transcription factor, Sox-18|journal=Nucleic Acids Research|volume=23|issue=14|pages=2626–2628|doi=10.1093/nar/23.14.2626|pmid=7651823|issn=0305-1048|pmc=307084}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pennisi|first1=David|last2=Gardner|first2=Jennifer|last3=Chambers|first3=Doreen|last4=Hosking|first4=Brett|last5=Peters|first5=Josephine|last6=Muscat|first6=George|last7=Abbott|first7=Catherine|last8=Koopman|first8=Peter|date=April 2000|title=Mutations in Sox18 underlie cardiovascular and hair follicle defects in ragged mice|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=24|issue=4|pages=434–437|doi=10.1038/74301|pmid=10742113|s2cid=24013687|issn=1061-4036}}</ref> a switch gene that directs formation of the lymphatic vessels,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=François|first1=Mathias|last2=Caprini|first2=Andrea|last3=Hosking|first3=Brett|last4=Orsenigo|first4=Fabrizio|last5=Wilhelm|first5=Dagmar|last6=Browne|first6=Catherine|last7=Paavonen|first7=Karri|last8=Karnezis|first8=Tara|last9=Shayan|first9=Ramin|date=2008-10-19|title=Sox18 induces development of the lymphatic vasculature in mice|journal=Nature|volume=456|issue=7222|pages=643–647|doi=10.1038/nature07391|pmid=18931657|bibcode=2008Natur.456..643F|s2cid=4416082|issn=0028-0836}}</ref> and is defective in humans with [[Hypotrichosis–lymphedema–telangiectasia syndrome|hypotrichosis-lymphedema-telangiectasia]] syndrome.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Irrthum|first1=Alexandre|last2=Devriendt|first2=Koenraad|last3=Chitayat|first3=David|last4=Matthijs|first4=Gert|last5=Glade|first5=Conrad|last6=Steijlen|first6=Peter M.|last7=Fryns|first7=Jean-Pierre|last8=Van Steensel|first8=Maurice A. M.|last9=Vikkula|first9=Miikka|date=June 2003|title=Mutations in the Transcription Factor Gene SOX18 Underlie Recessive and Dominant Forms of Hypotrichosis-Lymphedema-Telangiectasia|journal=The American Journal of Human Genetics|volume=72|issue=6|pages=1470–1478|doi=10.1086/375614|issn=0002-9297|pmc=1180307|pmid=12740761}}</ref>  Given the role of lymphatic vessels in tumour metastasis, Sox18 is being developed as a potential drug target for anti-metastatic cancer therapy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Overman|first1=Jeroen|last2=Fontaine|first2=Frank|last3=Moustaqil|first3=Mehdi|last4=Mittal|first4=Deepak|last5=Sierecki|first5=Emma|last6=Sacilotto|first6=Natalia|last7=Zuegg|first7=Johannes|last8=Robertson|first8=Avril AB|last9=Holmes|first9=Kelly|date=2017-01-31|title=Pharmacological targeting of the transcription factor SOX18 delays breast cancer in mice|journal=eLife|volume=6|doi=10.7554/elife.21221|issn=2050-084X|pmc=5283831|pmid=28137359 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Koopman found that the human and mouse genomes contain 20 Sox genes,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Schepers|first1=Goslik E.|last2=Teasdale|first2=Rohan D.|last3=Koopman|first3=Peter|date=August 2002|title=Twenty Pairs of Sox|journal=Developmental Cell|volume=3|issue=2|pages=167–170|doi=10.1016/s1534-5807(02)00223-x|pmid=12194848|issn=1534-5807|doi-access=free}}</ref> and he proposed the naming system for Sox genes that continues to be used today.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bowles|first1=Josephine|last2=Schepers|first2=Goslik|last3=Koopman|first3=Peter|date=November 2000|title=Phylogeny of the SOX Family of Developmental Transcription Factors Based on Sequence and Structural Indicators|journal=Developmental Biology|volume=227|issue=2|pages=239–255|doi=10.1006/dbio.2000.9883|pmid=11071752|issn=0012-1606|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Germ cell sex ===
Koopman's early work with Anne McLaren spawned an interest in the regulation of the [[germ cell]]s during fetal development—cells that later become sperm or oocytes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Koopman P. |title=The Curious World of Gonadal Development in Mammals. |journal=Current Topics in Developmental Biology |date=2016 |volume=116 |pages=537–545 |doi=10.1016/bs.ctdb.2015.12.009 |pmid=26970639|isbn=9780128029565 }}</ref> His group discovered that the vitamin A metabolite [[retinoic acid]] stimulates germ cells to enter [[meiosis]], a critical step in the formation of gametes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bowles|first1=Josephine|last2=Knight|first2=Deon|last3=Smith|first3=Christopher|last4=Wilhelm|first4=Dagmar|last5=Richman|first5=Joy|last6=Mamiya|first6=Satoru|last7=Yashiro|first7=Kenta|last8=Chawengsaksophak|first8=Kallayanee|last9=Wilson|first9=Megan J.|date=2006-04-28|title=Retinoid Signaling Determines Germ Cell Fate in Mice|journal=Science|volume=312|issue=5773|pages=596–600|doi=10.1126/science.1125691|issn=0036-8075|pmid=16574820|bibcode=2006Sci...312..596B|s2cid=2514848}}</ref> They also demonstrated that the developmental signaling molecule [[NODAL|Nodal]] and its receptor Cripto regulate male germ cell [[Cell potency|pluripotency]] in the fetal gonad,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Spiller|first1=Cassy M.|last2=Feng|first2=Chun-Wei|last3=Jackson|first3=Andrew|last4=Gillis|first4=Ad J. M.|last5=Rolland|first5=Antoine D.|last6=Looijenga|first6=Leendert H. J.|last7=Koopman|first7=Peter|last8=Bowles|first8=Josephine|date=2012-11-15|title=Endogenous Nodal signaling regulates germ cell potency during mammalian testis development|journal=Development|volume=139|issue=22|pages=4123–4132|doi=10.1242/dev.083006|issn=0950-1991|pmid=23034635|doi-access=free}}</ref> opening the way for new non-invasive diagnostics and targeted additional therapies for testicular cancers.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Spiller|first1=Cassy M.|last2=Bowles|first2=Josephine|last3=Koopman|first3=Peter|date=2013|title=Nodal/Cripto signaling in fetal male germ cell development: implications for testicular germ cell tumors|journal=The International Journal of Developmental Biology|volume=57|issue=2–3–4|pages=211–219|doi=10.1387/ijdb.130028pk|pmid=23784832|issn=0214-6282|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Intersex advocacy ===
With a growing interest in human variations of sex development (alternatively known as DSD, differences or [[disorders of sex development]], variations in sex characteristics, or [[intersex]]), Koopman began to engage with relevant clinicians and intersex advocacy and support groups. To cater for a need for unbiased information relating to the causes, types, impacts of DSD and options for affected people, Koopman authored a [http://dsdgenetics.org/ website], published under the auspices of the Australian [[National Health and Medical Research Council]]’s Research Program in Human DSD. He continues to work with the Australian Pediatric Endocrine Group and a range of advocacy groups to improve dialogue and management of these conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Peter A.|last2=Nordenström|first2=Anna|last3=Houk|first3=Christopher P.|last4=Ahmed|first4=S. Faisal|last5=Auchus|first5=Richard|last6=Baratz|first6=Arlene|last7=Baratz Dalke|first7=Katharine|last8=Liao|first8=Lih-Mei|last9=Lin-Su|first9=Karen|date=2016|title=Global Disorders of Sex Development Update since 2006: Perceptions, Approach and Care|journal=Hormone Research in Paediatrics|volume=85|issue=3|pages=158–180|doi=10.1159/000442975|pmid=26820577|issn=1663-2818|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Research integrity ===
From 2012 to 2017, Koopman worked as the University of Queensland's Executive Director of Research Integrity, providing academic stewardship of research integrity and managing allegations of research misconduct.

=== Equity and diversity ===
Koopman co-chairs the Equity and Diversity Reference Group of the Australian Academy of Science<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org.au/about-us/governance/standing-committees-council/equity-diversity-reference-group|title=Committee—Equity and Diversity Reference Group {{!}} Australian Academy of Science|website=www.science.org.au|access-date=2018-10-10}}</ref> and is a member of the Women in Health Science Working Committee of NHMRC Australia,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nhmrc.gov.au/research/women-health-science/women-health-science-working-committee|title=Women in health science working committee|last=|first=|date=|website=National Health and Medical Research Council|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> and is involved in developing the Decadal Plan for Women in STEM<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org.au/support/analysis/decadal-plans-science/decadal-plan-women-stem|title=Women in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) Decadal Plan {{!}} Australian Academy of Science|website=www.science.org.au|access-date=2018-10-10}}</ref> commissioned by the Australian Government.

== Other achievements ==
Koopman instigated the Australian Developmental Biology Workshop (2001- ), the Australian Sex Summit (2004- ), and the International Workshop on Sox Transcription Factors (2005 - ). He was organizer of the Cold Spring Harbor (USA) Workshop on Molecular Embryology of the Mouse (1995-1998), and Chair of the Gordon Research Conference on Germinal Stem Cell Biology (2017).

Koopman has trained 34 postdoctoral research staff and 28 PhD students. He has published more than 280 research papers that have been cited over 19,000 times.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://orcid.org/0000-0001-6939-0914|title=Peter Koopman (0000-0001-6939-0914) - ORCID {{!}} Connecting Research and Researchers|last=ORCID|website=orcid.org|access-date=2018-10-10}}</ref>
